questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An element of the p-block has the ground-state electronic configuration [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p⁵. The element is:

solution.concept: Valence-shell configuration of the p-block groups
solution.explanation: The valence shell is n = 5 with seven electrons (5s² 5p⁵), the configuration ns² np⁵ of group 17. The group 17 element of the fifth period is iodine (Z = 36 + 10 + 7 = 53).
solution.why_others_wrong: Tellurium is 5p⁴ (group 16), antimony 5p³ (group 15) and xenon 5p⁶ (group 18).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 17: electronic configuration

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In which group of the p-block do all the elements from the second period down to the fifth period exist as diatomic molecules in the free (elemental) state?

solution.concept: Molecular nature of the p-block elements
solution.explanation: The halogens F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ are all diatomic. In group 15 only nitrogen is diatomic (phosphorus forms P₄), in group 16 only oxygen is diatomic (sulphur forms S₈), and the noble gases are monoatomic.
steps: Group 17: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ → all diatomic
solution.why_others_wrong: Groups 15 and 16 have only their first member diatomic; group 18 elements are monoatomic.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 17 elements: physical properties

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The total number of unpaired electrons in the ground-state atoms of phosphorus (Z = 15), sulphur (Z = 16), chlorine (Z = 17) and argon (Z = 18), taken together, is:

solution.concept: Hund's rule applied to the np subshell of the p-block elements
solution.explanation: The 3p subshell holds three, four, five and six electrons in P, S, Cl and Ar. By Hund's rule the electrons occupy the three 3p orbitals singly before pairing.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 counts phosphorus only; 18 counts all the 3p electrons, paired or not; 9 takes S and Cl as having three unpaired electrons each, like P.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', electronic configuration of groups 15–18

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Every element placed in groups 13 to 18 of the periodic table has the valence-shell configuration ns² np¹⁻⁶.
Statement II: The number of valence electrons in an atom of a p-block element is equal to its group number.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: General configuration of the p-block elements
solution.explanation: The valence configuration ns² np¹⁻⁶ holds for the p-block elements except helium, which is placed in group 18 but has the configuration 1s². So Statement I ('every element') is false. A p-block element has (group number − 10) valence electrons, e.g. three for group 13 and seven for group 17, so Statement II is false.
steps: Helium (group 18) is 1s², with no p electrons → Statement I false
Valence electrons = group number − 10 (e.g. Cl, group 17 → 7) → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', p-block elements
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the atomic number of the element in List-I with the group of the periodic table to which it belongs in List-II.

List-I:
A. Z = 32
B. Z = 52
C. Z = 83
D. Z = 86

List-II:
I. Group 15
II. Group 18
III. Group 14
IV. Group 16

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Locating p-block elements from their electronic configurations
solution.explanation: Z = 32: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p² (germanium, group 14). Z = 52: [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p⁴ (tellurium, group 16). Z = 83: [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p³ (bismuth, group 15). Z = 86: [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p⁶ (radon, group 18).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange groups 15 and 16, or 14 and 16, or groups 15 and 18.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', electronic configurations and the periodic table
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Oxygen has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than sulphur.
Reason (R): The oxygen atom is very small, so an incoming electron is strongly repelled by the electrons already present in its compact 2p subshell.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Anomalous electron gain enthalpy of the first member of group 16
solution.explanation: Down a group the electron gain enthalpy normally becomes less negative, but oxygen (−141 kJ mol⁻¹) is less negative than sulphur (−200 kJ mol⁻¹). Because the oxygen atom is so compact, the added electron feels strong electron–electron repulsion, which outweighs its closeness to the nucleus. R is the reason for A.
steps: ΔegH: O −141, S −200 kJ mol⁻¹ → A true
Small 2p shell → strong interelectronic repulsion → R true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 16: electron gain enthalpy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Among the oxides of a group 14 element, the oxide in the higher oxidation state is more acidic than the oxide in the lower oxidation state.
Statement II: The tendency of the group 14 elements to form compounds in the +2 oxidation state decreases down the group from carbon to lead.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Oxidation states and nature of oxides in group 14
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that for group 14 the oxides in higher oxidation states are generally more acidic than those in lower oxidation states, so Statement I is true. Because of the inert pair effect, the +2 state becomes more important down the group (lead prefers +2), so Statement II states the trend the wrong way round.
steps: Higher oxidation state → more acidic oxide → Statement I true
Inert pair effect → +2 state more stable down the group → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 14: oxidation states and reactivity towards oxygen
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Lead has the ground-state configuration [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p² (Z = 82). The number of electrons in the outermost (sixth) shell of the Pb²⁺ ion is:

solution.concept: Inert pair effect in the configuration of Pb²⁺
solution.explanation: Pb²⁺ is formed by the loss of the two 6p electrons. The 6s² pair is retained (the inert pair), so the sixth shell of Pb²⁺ still holds two electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 is the count for the neutral atom; 0 treats Pb²⁺ as if all four valence electrons were lost (that is Pb⁴⁺); 18 is the count of the fifth shell (5s² 5p⁶ 5d¹⁰).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 14: electronic configuration and oxidation states

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following p-block elements has a completely filled 4f subshell in its ground state?

solution.concept: Filled inner subshells in the heavier p-block elements
solution.explanation: The 4f subshell is filled only after the 6s level, in the lanthanoids (Z = 58–71). Elements of the sixth period beyond the lanthanoids, such as lead ([Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p²), carry a filled 4f subshell. Tin, antimony and iodine belong to the fifth period and have no 4f electrons.
steps: 4f fills from Ce to Lu (6th period)
Sn, Sb, I (5th period) → [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5pⁿ, no 4f electrons
solution.why_others_wrong: Tin, antimony and iodine have a filled 4d subshell but an empty 4f subshell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', electronic configurations of the heavier elements

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An element X has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³. Which of the following statements about X is correct?

options.text: X is the most metallic element of its group.
The hydride XH₃ is a stronger base than ammonia.
Like nitrogen, X cannot show a covalency greater than four.

solution.concept: Identifying a group 15 element and applying group trends
solution.explanation: The configuration 4s² 4p³ is that of arsenic (group 15, period 4). Among the +3 oxides of group 15, those of nitrogen and phosphorus are acidic, those of arsenic and antimony are amphoteric, and that of bismuth is predominantly basic. Bismuth, not arsenic, is the most metallic member; the basicity of the hydrides falls from NH₃ down the group; and unlike nitrogen, arsenic has vacant d orbitals and can expand its covalency.
steps: NH₃ is the most basic hydride
solution.why_others_wrong: Bismuth is the most metallic element of group 15; AsH₃ is a much weaker base than NH₃; only nitrogen is limited to a covalency of four.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 15: trends in properties of oxides and hydrides
solution.final_answer: Option D: The oxide X₂O₃ is amphoteric.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following elements have a completely filled d subshell in the shell just inside the valence shell, i.e. an (n − 1)d¹⁰ subshell?
B (Z = 5), Al (Z = 13), Ga (Z = 31), In (Z = 49), C (Z = 6), Si (Z = 14), Ge (Z = 32), Sn (Z = 50)

solution.concept: Inner d¹⁰ subshells in groups 13 and 14
solution.explanation: The elements of the second and third periods have no d electrons at all. The members of groups 13 and 14 from the fourth period onwards come after a transition series, so they carry a filled (n − 1)d¹⁰ subshell: Ga and Ge (3d¹⁰), In and Sn (4d¹⁰).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 counts only the fifth-period elements; 6 wrongly includes Al and Si, whose shell inside the valence shell is the second shell (no d subshell); 8 counts every element.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', groups 13 and 14: electronic configuration

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the oxidation states of the group 14 elements are correct?

(a) Tin(II) compounds act as reducing agents.
(b) Lead(IV) compounds act as oxidising agents.
(c) Germanium forms stable compounds mainly in the +2 oxidation state.
(d) For carbon and silicon, the +2 oxidation state is more stable than the +4 state.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Inert pair effect and the redox behaviour of group 14 compounds
solution.explanation: Down group 14 the ns² pair becomes reluctant to take part in bonding, so the +2 state gains stability. Germanium forms stable compounds in the +4 state and only a few in +2. Tin shows both states, and Sn(II) readily changes to Sn(IV), so it is a reducing agent. For lead, +2 is the stable state, so Pb(IV) compounds are strong oxidising agents. Carbon and silicon are typically tetravalent (+4).
steps: (d) C and Si: +4 is the stable state → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (c) or (d), or leaves out one of the two true statements.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 14: oxidation states and trends in chemical reactivity

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The atomic radius of gallium is smaller than that of aluminium, although gallium lies below aluminium in group 13.
Reason (R): The ten 3d electrons in gallium shield the nucleus poorly, so its outer electrons experience a larger effective nuclear charge.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Anomaly in the atomic radii of group 13
solution.explanation: Atomic radii normally increase down a group, but gallium (135 pm) is smaller than aluminium (143 pm). Between aluminium and gallium a full 3d subshell is added; d electrons screen the nucleus poorly, so the increase in nuclear charge is not offset and the outer electrons are pulled in. R explains A.
steps: Al 143 pm, Ga 135 pm → A true
3d¹⁰ poor shielding → higher effective nuclear charge → R true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry (pre-2023 edition), 'The p-Block Elements', group 13: atomic radii
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts. Match the process in List-I with the catalyst used in it in List-II.

List-I:
A. Contact process (oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃)
B. Haber's process (synthesis of ammonia)
C. Catalytic hydrogenation
D. Reaction between iodide and persulphate ions

List-II:
I. Nickel
II. Fe³⁺ ions
III. Vanadium(V) oxide
IV. Finely divided iron

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Catalytic properties of transition metals and their compounds
solution.explanation: NCERT gives V₂O₅ (Contact process), finely divided iron (Haber's process) and nickel (catalytic hydrogenation) as examples of transition metal catalysts. The reaction 2I⁻ + S₂O₈²⁻ → I₂ + 2SO₄²⁻ is catalysed by Fe³⁺ ions, which are reduced by iodide and re-oxidised by persulphate.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange V₂O₅ with iron, nickel with Fe³⁺, or iron with nickel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', catalytic properties
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the aquated metal ion in List-I with its colour in aqueous solution in List-II.

List-I:
A. Cr³⁺
B. Fe³⁺
C. Co²⁺
D. Ni²⁺

List-II:
I. Green
II. Pink
III. Violet
IV. Yellow

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Colours of hydrated ions of the first transition series
solution.explanation: Colour arises from d–d transitions of the partly filled 3d subshell. NCERT lists the aquated ions: Cr³⁺ violet, Fe³⁺ yellow, Co²⁺ pink and Ni²⁺ green.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange the violet and green ions, or the yellow and pink ones.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', formation of coloured ions (table of colours)
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which lanthanoid has the ground-state electronic configuration [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹ 6s²?

solution.concept: Electronic configurations of the lanthanoids
solution.explanation: The configuration contains 54 + 14 + 1 + 2 = 71 electrons, which is lutetium, the last lanthanoid: the 4f subshell is full and one electron enters 5d. Ytterbium is [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 6s², gadolinium [Xe] 4f⁷ 5d¹ 6s² and cerium [Xe] 4f¹ 5d¹ 6s².
solution.why_others_wrong: Yb has no 5d electron (4f¹⁴ 6s²); Gd has only seven 4f electrons; Ce has one 4f electron.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', lanthanoids: electronic configurations

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The percentage of manganese by mass in potassium permanganate, KMnO₄, is (K = 39, Mn = 55, O = 16):

solution.concept: Percentage composition of potassium permanganate
solution.explanation: Molar mass of KMnO₄ = 39 + 55 + 4 × 16 = 158 g mol⁻¹, of which manganese contributes 55 g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 46.2% leaves potassium out of the molar mass; 24.7% is the percentage of potassium; 40.5% is the percentage of oxygen.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium permanganate

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In acidic solution, dichromate ions oxidise tin(II) to tin(IV) and are themselves reduced to Cr³⁺:
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 3Sn²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3Sn⁴⁺ + 7H₂O
The volume of 0.10 M SnCl₂ solution that is oxidised completely by 20.0 mL of 0.050 M K₂Cr₂O₇ solution is:

solution.concept: Stoichiometry of oxidation by acidified dichromate
solution.explanation: Each Cr₂O₇²⁻ gains six electrons (2Cr: +6 → +3), and each Sn²⁺ loses two electrons, so one dichromate ion oxidises three Sn²⁺ ions.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10.0 mL takes a 1 : 1 ratio and 20.0 mL a 1 : 2 ratio; 60.0 mL treats Sn²⁺ → Sn⁴⁺ as a one-electron change.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium dichromate: oxidising action (tin(II) salts)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Potassium dichromate cannot be used as a primary standard in volumetric analysis.
Statement II: The use of potassium permanganate for bleaching wool, cotton and silk and for decolourising oils depends on its strong oxidising power.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Uses of potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate
solution.explanation: NCERT states that potassium dichromate is used as a primary standard in volumetric analysis, so Statement I is false. NCERT also notes that the uses of KMnO₄ in bleaching textile fibres and decolourising oils depend on its strong oxidising power, so Statement II is true.
steps: K₂Cr₂O₇: a primary standard → Statement I false
KMnO₄: bleaching depends on oxidising power → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate (uses)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ground-state configuration of uranium (Z = 92) is [Rn] 5f³ 6d¹ 7s². The number of 5f electrons in the U⁴⁺ ion is:

solution.concept: Configurations of actinoid ions
solution.explanation: On ionisation the 7s electrons are lost first, then the 6d electron, and only then 5f electrons. Removing four electrons from U takes away 7s², 6d¹ and one 5f electron, leaving 5f².
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 is the 5f count of the neutral atom (or of U³⁺); 1 and 0 remove too many 5f electrons, as if the 7s or 6d electrons were kept.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', actinoids: electronic configurations

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The highest fluorides formed by vanadium and chromium are VF₅ and CrF₆ respectively.
Reason (R): Fluorine stabilises high oxidation states only through the high lattice energy of ionic fluorides.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Stabilisation of high oxidation states by fluorine
solution.explanation: NCERT lists VF₅ and CrF₆ as the halides showing the highest oxidation states of these metals, so A is true. NCERT explains that fluorine stabilises the highest oxidation state either through a higher lattice energy (as in CoF₃) or through higher bond enthalpy terms in the higher covalent fluorides (as in VF₅ and CrF₆). The word 'only' makes R false, and the covalent fluorides VF₅ and CrF₆ are exactly the cases R leaves out.
steps: Two factors: lattice energy (CoF₃) or bond enthalpy (VF₅, CrF₆)
R claims lattice energy only → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', oxidation states (halides of the 3d metals)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the oxides of vanadium and chromium are correct?

(a) V₂O₅ is amphoteric, though mainly acidic.
(b) CrO₃ is an acidic oxide.
(c) CrO is a basic oxide.
(d) V₂O₃ is an acidic oxide.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Acid–base character of transition metal oxides and the oxidation state
solution.explanation: For a given metal, the oxide becomes less basic and more acidic as the oxidation state rises. For vanadium the change is from basic V₂O₃ to less basic V₂O₄ and to amphoteric V₂O₅, which is mainly acidic. For chromium, CrO is basic, Cr₂O₃ amphoteric and CrO₃ acidic (it gives H₂CrO₄ and H₂Cr₂O₇).
steps: (d) V₂O₃ (+3, lowest state) is basic → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) are wrong, and (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', oxides of the 3d metals

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 0.20 g of an impure sample of potassium dichromate is dissolved in dilute H₂SO₄ and titrated with 0.10 M Fe²⁺ solution. 30.0 mL of the Fe²⁺ solution is needed to reduce all the dichromate to Cr³⁺. Assuming the impurities do not react, the percentage purity of the sample is (K = 39, Cr = 52, O = 16, Na = 23):

solution.concept: Redox titration of dichromate with iron(II)
solution.explanation: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. One dichromate ion accepts six electrons, each Fe²⁺ gives one, so 6 mol of Fe²⁺ reduce 1 mol of dichromate.
solution.why_others_wrong: 88.2% uses the 1 : 5 ratio of permanganate; 36.8% counts six Fe²⁺ per chromium atom (1 : 12); 65.5% uses the molar mass of sodium dichromate (262).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', potassium dichromate: oxidising action (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following ions have a half-filled 4f subshell (4f⁷)?
Sm²⁺, Eu²⁺, Eu³⁺, Gd³⁺, Tb⁴⁺, Dy³⁺
(Atomic numbers: Sm 62, Eu 63, Gd 64, Tb 65, Dy 66; Xe = 54. The atoms are Sm [Xe] 4f⁶ 6s², Eu [Xe] 4f⁷ 6s², Gd [Xe] 4f⁷ 5d¹ 6s², Tb [Xe] 4f⁹ 6s², Dy [Xe] 4f¹⁰ 6s².)

solution.concept: Configurations of lanthanoid ions in the +2, +3 and +4 states
solution.explanation: A lanthanoid ion Lnⁿ⁺ loses the 6s electrons first, then any 5d electron, then 4f electrons, so its number of 4f electrons is Z − 54 − n.
solution.shortcut: 4f⁷ means Z − n = 61: Eu²⁺ (63 − 2), Gd³⁺ (64 − 3) and Tb⁴⁺ (65 − 4).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses one of the three f⁷ ions (often Tb⁴⁺); 4 or 5 wrongly include Eu³⁺ or Sm²⁺ (4f⁶) or Dy³⁺ (4f⁹).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', lanthanoids: electronic configurations and oxidation states

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Ce(IV) is used as an oxidising agent in analytical work, although the value E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) = +1.74 V suggests that it could oxidise water.
Reason (R): The reaction of Ce⁴⁺ ions with water is very slow.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Thermodynamic and kinetic factors in the chemistry of cerium(IV)
solution.explanation: Ce⁴⁺ (noble gas configuration) is a strong oxidant that reverts to the common +3 state. Its E° value shows that oxidising water is thermodynamically favourable, but the reaction is very slow, so Ce(IV) solutions remain usable and Ce(IV) is a good analytical reagent. The slow rate is exactly why A holds.
steps: E° = +1.74 V → oxidation of water feasible
Rate of that reaction is very slow
So Ce(IV) solutions are usable → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', lanthanoids: oxidation states
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the oxidation states of the f-block elements are correct?

(a) Pr, Nd, Tb and Dy also show the +4 oxidation state, but only in oxides of the type MO₂.
(b) The maximum oxidation state shown by protactinium is +5.
(c) In general, the +2 oxidation state of the lanthanoids is more stable than the +3 state.
(d) All the actinoids show only the +3 oxidation state.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Oxidation states of the lanthanoids and actinoids
solution.explanation: The common oxidation state of the lanthanoids is +3; +2 and +4 occur less often, and Pr, Nd, Tb and Dy show +4 only in their oxides MO₂. Among the actinoids, the maximum oxidation state rises from +4 in Th to +5, +6 and +7 in Pa, U and Np, and then decreases. So the actinoids show a wide range of states, not +3 alone.
steps: (c) +3 is the common, most stable state → false
(d) Th +4, U up to +6, Np up to +7 → false
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (c) or (d), or leave out (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'The d- and f-Block Elements', lanthanoids and actinoids: oxidation states

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following ligands can bind to a metal ion through either of two different kinds of donor atom (one at a time)?

solution.concept: Ambidentate ligands
solution.explanation: A ligand that can ligate through two different atoms is ambidentate. The thiocyanate ion can bind through sulphur (M–SCN) or through nitrogen (M–NCS). Ethane-1,2-diamine and oxalate are didentate: they bind through two atoms of the same element (two N or two O) at the same time. Ammonia is unidentate.
steps: SCN⁻: donor atom S or N → ambidentate
en: two N at once → didentate
C₂O₄²⁻: two O at once → didentate
solution.why_others_wrong: en and oxalate use two donor atoms of the same kind simultaneously (chelation); NH₃ has only one donor atom.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', definitions: ligands (ambidentate ligands)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the complex Na₃[Co(NO₂)₆], each nitrite ligand is bonded to cobalt through its nitrogen atom. The IUPAC name of the compound is:

solution.concept: Naming an anionic coordination entity
solution.explanation: The cation is named first. Oxidation state of Co: x + 6(−1) = −3 → x = +3. Because the complex ion is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate: cobaltate(III). The N-bonded nitrite ligand is nitrito-N.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'cobalt(III)' omits the -ate ending needed for an anionic entity; (II) is the wrong oxidation state; the cation must be named first.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', nomenclature of coordination compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Valence bond theory does not make exact predictions about whether a 4-coordinate complex will be tetrahedral or square planar.
Statement II: Valence bond theory gives a quantitative interpretation of the thermodynamic and kinetic stabilities of coordination compounds.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Limitations of valence bond theory
solution.explanation: NCERT lists among the limitations of VBT that it does not make exact predictions regarding the tetrahedral and square planar structures of 4-coordinate complexes (Statement I true) and that it does not give a quantitative interpretation of the thermodynamic or kinetic stabilities of coordination compounds (Statement II false).
steps: Statement I: a listed limitation → true
Statement II: VBT cannot do this → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', limitations of valence bond theory
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the ligand in List-I with the name used for it in the IUPAC name of a coordination compound (List-II).

List-I:
A. C₂O₄²⁻
B. H₂N–CH₂–CH₂–NH₂
C. OH⁻
D. CN⁻

List-II:
I. Cyanido
II. Oxalato
III. Ethane-1,2-diamine
IV. Hydroxido

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Names of ligands in IUPAC nomenclature
solution.explanation: Anionic ligands take names ending in -o (oxalato, hydroxido, cyanido), while neutral ligands keep their names (ethane-1,2-diamine), apart from the special names aqua, ammine, carbonyl and nitrosyl.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange the names of the two neutral/anionic ligands or of hydroxido and cyanido.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', nomenclature: naming of ligands
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the complex ion [Cr(NH₃)₄(C₂O₄)]ˣ, chromium is in the +3 oxidation state and the oxalate ion acts as a didentate ligand. The charge x on the complex ion and the coordination number of chromium are, respectively:

solution.concept: Charge and coordination number of a coordination entity
solution.explanation: Charge = oxidation state of the metal + sum of ligand charges. Coordination number = number of donor atoms bonded to the metal; a didentate ligand supplies two.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 counts oxalate as unidentate; −1 adds the oxalate charge with the wrong sign; +3 ignores the charge of the oxalate ion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', coordination number and oxidation number

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The formula of pentaamminecarbonatocobalt(III) chloride is:

solution.concept: Writing a formula from an IUPAC name
solution.explanation: The coordination sphere contains five NH₃ ligands and one carbonate ion bonded to Co³⁺. Its charge is +3 + 5(0) + (−2) = +1, so one chloride ion is needed as the counter ion.
solution.why_others_wrong: [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]CO₃ is pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) carbonate (an ionisation isomer); two chlorides would not balance a +1 ion; [Co(NH₃)₄(CO₃)]Cl has only four ammine ligands.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', formulas and nomenclature of mononuclear compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following are correct rules for writing the formula of a mononuclear coordination entity?

(a) The central atom is listed first.
(b) The ligands are then listed in alphabetical order, irrespective of their charge.
(c) For an abbreviated polydentate ligand, the first letter of the abbreviation decides its place in the alphabetical order.
(d) The charge of a complex ion is written inside the square brackets.
(e) A space is left between the ligands and the metal within the coordination sphere.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Rules for writing formulas of coordination entities
solution.explanation: NCERT's rules: the central atom is listed first; ligands follow in alphabetical order, and their place does not depend on charge; abbreviated polydentate ligands are placed by the first letter of the abbreviation; the entire entity is enclosed in square brackets with no space between ligands and metal; the charge of a complex ion is written outside the brackets as a right superscript.
steps: (d) charge goes outside the brackets → false
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options contain (d) or (e), or leave out one of the true rules.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', formulas of mononuclear coordination entities

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In the extraction of gold, the soluble complex [Au(CN)₂]⁻ is treated with zinc:
2[Au(CN)₂]⁻ + Zn → [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ + 2Au
The mass of gold recovered when 1.30 g of zinc reacts completely is (Zn = 65, Au = 197):

solution.concept: Stoichiometry of the recovery of gold from its cyanide complex
solution.explanation: Zinc displaces gold from the complex; each zinc atom releases two gold atoms.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.94 g takes Zn : Au as 1 : 1; 15.76 g as 1 : 4; 1.97 g inverts the ratio (2 : 1).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', importance and applications (extraction of gold)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In Mn₂(CO)₁₀, two Mn(CO)₅ units are joined by a manganese–manganese bond.
Statement II: Co₂(CO)₈ contains a cobalt–cobalt bond, which is bridged by two CO groups.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Structures of polynuclear metal carbonyls
solution.explanation: Besides the mononuclear carbonyls Ni(CO)₄, Fe(CO)₅ and Cr(CO)₆, NCERT shows two dinuclear carbonyls: Mn₂(CO)₁₀, made of two square pyramidal Mn(CO)₅ units joined by a Mn–Mn bond, and Co₂(CO)₈, which has a Co–Co bond bridged by two CO groups. Both statements are true.
steps: Mn₂(CO)₁₀: Mn–Mn bond → Statement I true
Co₂(CO)₈: Co–Co bond with two bridging CO → Statement II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', bonding in metal carbonyls (structures)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The spectrochemical series is an experimentally determined series, based on the absorption of light by complexes with different ligands.
Reason (R): Carbon monoxide lies at the strong-field end of the spectrochemical series.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Origin of the spectrochemical series
solution.explanation: A is NCERT's description of how the series is obtained: from absorption spectra of complexes of a metal ion with different ligands. R is also true, but it only states the position of one ligand in the series; it says nothing about how the series is determined. So R does not explain A.
steps: A: series obtained from absorption of light → true
R: CO causes the largest splitting → true
R is a fact about the series, not the reason for A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', crystal field theory (spectrochemical series)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Metal ions give characteristic colour reactions with chelating reagents such as EDTA, dimethylglyoxime, α-nitroso-β-naphthol and cupron, because coordination entities are formed. These reactions are used mainly for:

options.text: purifying metals by forming volatile complexes
the detection and estimation of metal ions
electroplating articles with a smooth coating of metal
removing excess metal ions from the body by chelate therapy

solution.concept: Coordination compounds in chemical analysis
solution.explanation: NCERT states that colour reactions of metal ions with ligands, especially chelating ligands, form the basis of their detection and estimation by classical and instrumental methods of analysis; EDTA, DMG, α-nitroso-β-naphthol and cupron are examples of such reagents.
solution.why_others_wrong: Purification uses volatile complexes such as Ni(CO)₄; electroplating uses cyanido complexes; chelate therapy uses EDTA, D-penicillamine or desferrioxime B, not these colour reactions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', importance and applications (qualitative and quantitative analysis)
solution.final_answer: Option B: the detection and estimation of metal ions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Counting geometrical and linkage isomers together, how many isomers are possible for the octahedral complex ion [Co(NH₃)₄Cl(NO₂)]⁺? (No optical isomer exists for this ion.)

solution.concept: Combining geometrical and linkage isomerism
solution.explanation: [Co(NH₃)₄Cl(NO₂)]⁺ is of the type [MA₄BC], which has cis and trans forms. Independently, the ambidentate nitrite ligand may be bonded through N (nitrito-N) or through O (nitrito-O). Each geometrical form can carry either linkage.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 counts only one kind of isomerism; 3 forgets one combination; 6 adds non-existent optical isomers.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', isomerism in coordination compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the complex ion in List-I with its hybridisation and number of unpaired electrons, according to valence bond theory, in List-II. (Atomic numbers: Cr 24, Fe 26, Co 27, Pt 78)

List-I:
A. [CoCl₄]²⁻ (tetrahedral)
B. [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (high spin)
C. [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺ (square planar)
D. [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺

List-II:
I. d²sp³, three unpaired electrons
II. dsp², no unpaired electron
III. sp³d², five unpaired electrons
IV. sp³, three unpaired electrons

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Hybridisation and magnetic behaviour from valence bond theory
solution.explanation: Co²⁺ (3d⁷) in tetrahedral [CoCl₄]²⁻ uses sp³ hybrids and keeps three unpaired electrons. High-spin Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) keeps five unpaired electrons and uses outer 4d orbitals (sp³d²). Pt²⁺ (5d⁸) in a square planar complex pairs its electrons and uses dsp² hybrids, so it is diamagnetic. Cr³⁺ (3d³) has two vacant inner 3d orbitals for d²sp³ hybridisation and three unpaired electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange the two complexes with three unpaired electrons, or the inner and outer orbital octahedral complexes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', valence bond theory and magnetic properties
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) [Ni(CO)₄] is a neutral coordination entity.
(b) In K₃[Al(C₂O₄)₃], the coordination number of aluminium is 6.
(c) The EDTA⁴⁻ ion binds a metal ion through two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms.
(d) In [Co(en)₃]³⁺, the coordination number of cobalt is 3.
(e) The oxidation state of iron in [Fe(CO)₅] is +2.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Charge, denticity, coordination number and oxidation state
solution.explanation: [Ni(CO)₄] has Ni(0) and neutral CO ligands, so it is neutral. Three didentate oxalate ions give Al six donor atoms. EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate: two amine nitrogen atoms and four carboxylate oxygen atoms. Three didentate en ligands give cobalt a coordination number of 6, not 3. CO is neutral and [Fe(CO)₅] is uncharged, so iron is in the zero oxidation state.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (d) or (e), or leave out (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', definitions (denticity, coordination number, oxidation number)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ is a low-spin complex with only one unpaired electron.
Reason (R): The oxalate ion is a weak-field ligand, so for Fe³⁺ in this complex Δo is smaller than the pairing energy P.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: High-spin and low-spin complexes of a d⁵ ion
solution.explanation: Oxalate lies below water in the spectrochemical series, so it produces a small Δo. For Fe³⁺ (3d⁵), Δo < P means the electrons occupy t₂g and eg singly (t₂g³ eg²): the complex is high spin with five unpaired electrons. A is false and R is true.
steps: Weak-field oxalate → Δo < P → t₂g³ eg²
Five unpaired electrons → high spin → A false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Coordination Compounds', crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text: In Dumas' method for estimating nitrogen, the gaseous products are passed over a heated copper gauze, and the nitrogen gas is then collected over:

options.text: an aqueous solution of potassium hydroxide

solution.concept: Dumas' method for nitrogen
solution.explanation: The compound is heated with copper(II) oxide in an atmosphere of CO₂, giving CO₂, H₂O and nitrogen (with some oxides of nitrogen). The hot copper gauze reduces the oxides of nitrogen to N₂. The gas is collected over aqueous KOH, which absorbs the carbon dioxide, so only nitrogen is measured.
steps: CuO oxidises C and H to CO₂ and H₂O
Cu gauze: oxides of N → N₂
KOH(aq) absorbs CO₂ → pure N₂ collected
solution.why_others_wrong: Water would not remove CO₂; conc. H₂SO₄ and anhydrous CaCl₂ absorb water vapour, not CO₂.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', estimation of nitrogen (Dumas method)
solution.final_answer: Option B: an aqueous solution of potassium hydroxide

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text: In a thin layer chromatography experiment, the solvent front rises 12.0 cm from the base line. Two components A and B of a mixture have Rf values of 0.65 and 0.40. The distance between the centres of the two spots on the plate is:

solution.concept: Retardation factor in TLC
solution.explanation: Rf = distance moved by the substance / distance moved by the solvent, both from the base line. So each spot lies at Rf × 12.0 cm from the base line.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.25 cm takes the difference of the Rf values as a distance; 12.6 cm adds the two distances; 6.3 cm averages them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', chromatography (TLC, Rf)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The nitrogen of nitrobenzene cannot be estimated by Kjeldahl's method.
Reason (R): During digestion in Kjeldahl's method, the nitrogen of nitro compounds is converted into sodium cyanide.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Limitations of Kjeldahl's method
solution.explanation: Kjeldahl's method works only when the nitrogen of the compound is converted into ammonium sulphate on heating with concentrated H₂SO₄. NCERT notes that the nitrogen of nitro and azo groups and of ring nitrogen (as in pyridine) does not change to ammonium sulphate, so A is true. No sodium is used in this digestion; conversion into sodium cyanide happens in sodium fusion (Lassaigne's test), so R is false.
steps: Nitro N is not converted into (NH₄)₂SO₄ → A true
NaCN forms in Lassaigne's test, not in Kjeldahl digestion → R false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', Kjeldahl's method
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds
questions.question_text: 0.30 g of an organic compound containing C, H, N and O gave 0.22 g of CO₂ and 0.18 g of H₂O on complete combustion. In a Kjeldahl estimation, the ammonia obtained from another 0.30 g of the compound exactly neutralised 50.0 mL of 0.10 M H₂SO₄. The molar mass of the compound is 60 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is (C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, O = 16):

solution.concept: Molecular formula from combustion and Kjeldahl data
solution.explanation: Moles of C come from CO₂, moles of H from twice the moles of H₂O, and moles of N from twice the moles of H₂SO₄ (2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄). Oxygen is found by difference.
steps: C : H : N : O = 1 : 4 : 2 : 1 → CH₄N₂O (M = 60) → molecular formula CH₄N₂O (urea)
solution.why_others_wrong: CH₄NO forgets that one H₂SO₄ takes two NH₃; CH₂N₂O takes the moles of H equal to the moles of water; C₂H₈N₄O₂ doubles the formula, ignoring the molar mass of 60.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', quantitative analysis

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: The IUPAC name of CH₂=CH–C≡CH is:

solution.concept: Numbering a chain containing both a double and a triple bond
solution.explanation: Numbering from either end gives the multiple bonds the locants 1 and 3. When there is such a tie, the double bond is given the lower number. The name ends in -yne, with -en- placed before it: but-1-en-3-yne.
steps: Lowest locants: {1, 3} from either end → tie
Tie → double bond gets the lower locant (1)
solution.why_others_wrong: But-3-en-1-yne gives the triple bond the lower number in a tie; 'yn-ene' reverses the order of the endings; 'dienyne' wrongly implies two double bonds.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', IUPAC nomenclature (compounds with multiple bonds)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the common name of the alkyl group in List-I with its structure in List-II.

List-I:
A. Isopropyl
B. sec-Butyl
C. Isobutyl
D. tert-Butyl

List-II:
I. (CH₃)₃C–
II. (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–
III. (CH₃)₂CH–
IV. CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Common names of branched alkyl groups
solution.explanation: Isopropyl is attached through the middle carbon of propane. sec-Butyl is attached through a secondary carbon of a straight four-carbon chain. Isobutyl, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂–, is attached through the CH₂ of the branched chain. tert-Butyl is attached through the tertiary carbon.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange sec-butyl with isobutyl, isopropyl with isobutyl, or isobutyl with tert-butyl.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of alkyl groups
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following compounds are ketones?
CH₃COCH₃, CH₃CHO, CH₃COOCH₃, C₆H₅COCH₃, CH₃CONH₂, cyclohexanone, CH₃COOH

solution.concept: Recognising functional groups
solution.explanation: A ketone has the >C=O group bonded to two carbon atoms. In an aldehyde one of the groups is H; in esters, amides and acids the carbonyl carbon is also bonded to O or N.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 or 5 count the ester, amide or acid as ketones because they contain C=O; 2 misses acetophenone or the cyclic ketone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', functional groups

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In IUPAC nomenclature, the prefix 'cyclo' is used for alicyclic compounds, as in cyclohexane.
Statement II: A carbon atom bonded to three other carbon atoms is called a tertiary (3°) carbon atom.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Nomenclature of cyclic compounds and classification of carbon atoms
solution.explanation: Saturated monocyclic compounds are named by adding 'cyclo' to the name of the corresponding straight-chain alkane. A carbon atom is called primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary when it is bonded to one, two, three or four other carbon atoms. Both statements are true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of cyclic compounds
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: The group C₆H₅–CH₂– is called:

solution.concept: Names of aryl and arylalkyl groups
solution.explanation: C₆H₅– is phenyl. When a CH₂ group links the benzene ring to the rest of the molecule, the group C₆H₅CH₂– is benzyl (as in the benzyl carbocation, C₆H₅CH₂⁺).
solution.why_others_wrong: Phenyl lacks the CH₂ group; benzoyl contains C=O; tolyl is a methyl-substituted phenyl group attached through the ring.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', reactive intermediates (benzyl carbocation)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: A compound contains an ester group (–COOR), a nitrile group (–CN), an amide group (–CONH₂) and an aldehyde group (–CHO). In its IUPAC name, the group cited as the suffix (the principal functional group) is:

solution.concept: Order of seniority of functional groups
solution.explanation: NCERT's order of preference is –COOH, –SO₃H, –COOR, –COCl, –CONH₂, –CN, –HC=O, >C=O, –OH, –NH₂, >C=C<, –C≡C–. Of the groups present, the ester comes first, so it is the principal group; the others are named as prefixes.
solution.why_others_wrong: Amide, nitrile and aldehyde groups all rank below the ester group.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of polyfunctional compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following are addition reactions?
(i) CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ (in CCl₄) → BrCH₂–CH₂Br
(ii) CH₄ + Cl₂ (light) → CH₃Cl + HCl
(iii) CH₃CHO + HCN → CH₃CH(OH)CN
(iv) CH₃CH₂Br + alcoholic KOH → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O
(v) C₆H₆ + HNO₃ (conc. H₂SO₄) → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O
(vi) HC≡CH + HCl → CH₂=CHCl

solution.concept: Classifying organic reactions
solution.explanation: In an addition reaction two molecules combine to give a single product, with no atom or group lost; the multiple bond (C=C, C≡C or C=O) is used up.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses the nucleophilic addition to C=O or the addition to C≡C; 4 counts the elimination or a substitution as addition.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', types of organic reactions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Water cannot act as a nucleophile because it is a neutral molecule.
Reason (R): Neutral molecules having an unshared pair of electrons, such as H₂O and R₃N, can act as nucleophiles.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Neutral nucleophiles
solution.explanation: A nucleophile is a species that brings an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre. It need not be negatively charged: NCERT lists neutral molecules with lone pairs, such as H₂O, R₃N: and R₂NH, as nucleophiles. So A is false and R is true.
steps: A nucleophile needs an available electron pair, not a charge
H₂O has two lone pairs on O → nucleophile
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nucleophiles and electrophiles
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following IUPAC names are correct?

(a) CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CN: butanenitrile
(b) CH₃–CH₂–CONH₂: propanamide
(c) CH₃–COO–CH₃: methyl methanoate
(d) (CH₃)₂CH–COOH: 2-methylpropanoic acid
(e) CH₃–CH₂–COO–CH₃: ethyl ethanoate

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Naming nitriles, amides, esters and acids
solution.explanation: In nitriles and amides the carbon of the functional group is counted in the parent chain. An ester R′COOR is named as alkyl alkanoate, the alkyl group R coming from the alcohol and the alkanoate from the acid.
steps: (a) four C including CN → butanenitrile → correct
(c) acid part has two C → methyl ethanoate → incorrect
(e) acid part propanoate, alcohol part methyl → methyl propanoate → incorrect
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (c) or (e), or leave out (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', IUPAC nomenclature of functional compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In an organic reaction, the reactant that supplies carbon to the new bond being formed is called the substrate.
Statement II: In the reaction CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻, the hydroxide ion is the substrate.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Substrate and reagent
solution.explanation: NCERT defines the substrate as the reactant that supplies carbon to the new bond, and the other reactant as the reagent. In the hydrolysis of CH₃Br, the new C–O bond gets its carbon from CH₃Br, so CH₃Br is the substrate and OH⁻ is the attacking reagent (a nucleophile).
steps: Carbon of the new C–O bond comes from CH₃Br → CH₃Br is the substrate
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', fundamental concepts in organic reaction mechanism
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In propenal, CH₂=CH–CHO, the terminal carbon atom (C-3) carries a partial positive charge.
Reason (R): The –CHO group withdraws π electrons from the C=C bond by its −R (resonance) effect.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: −R effect of a carbonyl group in a conjugated system
solution.explanation: In CH₂=CH–CH=O the π electrons of C=C are delocalised towards the electronegative oxygen. One canonical structure is ⁺CH₂–CH=CH–O⁻, so the terminal carbon becomes electron-deficient. This delocalisation is the −R effect of the –CHO group, so R explains A.
steps: Cause: −R effect of –CHO → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', resonance effect
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: A benzene ring carries a –CH₃ group, a –Cl group on the carbon next to it, and a –NO₂ group para to the –CH₃ group. The IUPAC name of the compound is:

solution.concept: Naming polysubstituted benzene derivatives
solution.explanation: The ring is numbered to give the substituents the lowest set of locants, and the prefixes are written in alphabetical order. Numbering from the CH₃ carbon towards Cl gives {1, 2, 4}; every other numbering gives a higher set (e.g. {1, 2, 5} or {1, 3, 4}).
solution.why_others_wrong: {1, 2, 5} and {1, 3, 4} are not the lowest locant sets; '4-nitro-2-chloro-1-methyl' does not list the prefixes alphabetically.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of substituted benzene compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text: The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CHO is:

solution.concept: Naming a polyfunctional compound
solution.explanation: The aldehyde group is senior to –OH, so the suffix is -al and C-1 is the CHO carbon. The chain of five carbons carries two methyl groups on C-2 and an –OH on C-4. Prefixes are written alphabetically: hydroxy before dimethyl ('di' is ignored in alphabetising).
solution.why_others_wrong: '2,2-Dimethyl-4-hydroxy' ignores alphabetical order; '2-hydroxy-4,4-dimethyl' numbers from the wrong end; the '-ol' name wrongly treats –OH as the principal group.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of polyfunctional compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following are correct rules of IUPAC nomenclature?

(a) The prefixes iso- and neo- are treated as part of the fundamental name of an alkyl group when substituents are arranged alphabetically.
(b) The prefixes sec- and tert- are taken into account when substituents are arranged alphabetically.
(c) If two chains of equal length are possible, the chain with the greater number of side chains is chosen as the parent chain.
(d) The chain is numbered so that the substituents get the highest possible locants.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Finer rules of IUPAC nomenclature
solution.explanation: NCERT states that iso- and neo- are part of the fundamental name of the alkyl group (isopropyl is alphabetised under 'i'), whereas sec- and tert- are not (tert-butyl is alphabetised under 'b'). When two chains are of equal size, the one with more side chains is selected. Numbering always aims at the lowest locants.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (b) or (d) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', IUPAC rules for branched alkanes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the group attached to a benzene ring in List-I with its electronic effects in List-II.

List-I:
A. –NH₂
B. –Cl
C. –NO₂
D. –CH₃

List-II:
I. −I and +R, the +R effect being dominant
II. −I and +R, the −I effect being dominant
III. −I and −R
IV. +I and hyperconjugation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Inductive and resonance effects of substituents
solution.explanation: –NH₂ is more electronegative than carbon (−I) but its lone pair is delocalised into the ring (+R), and the +R effect dominates, so it activates the ring. A halogen also shows −I and +R, but here −I dominates, so the ring is deactivated. –NO₂ withdraws electrons both inductively and by resonance. –CH₃ releases electrons by the +I effect and hyperconjugation.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange –NH₂ and –Cl (which differ in which effect dominates), –Cl and –NO₂, or –NO₂ and –CH₃.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', inductive and resonance effects
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In how many of the following compounds is the –OH group NOT the principal functional group (i.e. it is cited as the prefix 'hydroxy')?
HO–CH₂–CH₂–COOH, HO–CH₂–CHO, HO–CH₂–CH₂–NH₂, HO–CH₂–CH=CH₂, HO–CH₂–CH₂–CN, HO–CH₂–CO–CH₃

solution.concept: Seniority of –OH among functional groups
solution.explanation: –OH ranks below –COOH, –CN, –CHO and >C=O, but above –NH₂ and the C=C bond. So –OH is a prefix (hydroxy) only when one of the higher groups is present.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 wrongly ranks –NH₂ above –OH; 3 misses the nitrile or ketone; 2 ranks –OH above >C=O and –CN.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', nomenclature of polyfunctional compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the carbocation in List-I with the main factor that stabilises its positive charge in List-II.

List-I:
A. CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺
B. C₆H₅–CH₂⁺
C. (CH₃)₃C⁺
D. CH₃–CH₂⁺

List-II:
I. Delocalisation of the charge over the benzene ring
II. Delocalisation of the charge through an adjacent C=C bond
III. Hyperconjugation involving nine C–H bonds
IV. Hyperconjugation involving three C–H bonds

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Stabilisation of carbocations by resonance and hyperconjugation
solution.explanation: The allyl and benzyl carbocations are stabilised by resonance: the vacant p orbital overlaps with the π system of the adjacent C=C bond or of the benzene ring. In (CH₃)₃C⁺ three methyl groups provide nine C–H bonds for hyperconjugation; in CH₃CH₂⁺ one methyl group provides three.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes interchange the allyl and benzyl cations or the numbers of C–H bonds.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques', carbocations and hyperconjugation
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Rotation about the C–C single bond of ethane gives an infinite number of spatial arrangements. Those arrangements other than the staggered and the eclipsed forms are called:

solution.concept: Conformations of ethane
solution.explanation: The staggered and eclipsed forms are the two extreme conformations of ethane. NCERT calls all the other, intermediate conformations skew conformations.
solution.why_others_wrong: Staggered and eclipsed are the two extreme conformations themselves; conformations are not geometrical isomers, which arise from restricted rotation about a double bond.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', conformations of ethane

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Methane cannot be prepared by Kolbe's electrolytic method.
Statement II: Like alkenes, alkynes such as but-2-yne show geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism about the triple bond.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Kolbe's method and the geometry of alkynes
solution.explanation: In Kolbe's electrolysis two alkyl radicals R• from RCOO⁻ couple to give R–R, so the product always has an even number of carbon atoms (at least two); methane cannot be obtained. The C≡C unit and the two atoms attached to it are linear, so there is only one way to arrange the substituents and no cis–trans isomerism.
steps: Kolbe: 2RCOO⁻ → R–R (+ 2CO₂) → smallest product ethane → Statement I true
Alkyne: linear C–C≡C–C → no cis/trans forms → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', preparation of alkanes (Kolbe's electrolytic method); structure of triple bond
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Ethane is prepared by heating sodium propanoate with soda lime:
CH₃CH₂COONa + NaOH → CH₃–CH₃ + Na₂CO₃ (CaO)
The minimum mass of sodium propanoate needed to obtain 2.24 L of ethane, measured at STP, is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23; molar volume at STP = 22.4 L mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Decarboxylation of sodium salts of carboxylic acids
solution.explanation: The sodium salt loses CO₂ (as Na₂CO₃) and gives an alkane with one carbon atom fewer. One mole of sodium propanoate gives one mole of ethane.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.2 g uses sodium ethanoate (which gives methane, not ethane); 19.2 g assumes two moles of salt per mole of ethane, as in Kolbe's electrolysis; 4.8 g halves the amount.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', preparation of alkanes (decarboxylation)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Ethene is passed into cold, dilute, aqueous alkaline potassium permanganate (Baeyer's reagent), which converts it into ethane-1,2-diol. The mass of the diol formed from 5.6 g of ethene, assuming complete conversion, is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.concept: Oxidation of alkenes by Baeyer's reagent
solution.explanation: Each C=C unit adds two –OH groups: CH₂=CH₂ → HOCH₂–CH₂OH. One mole of ethene gives one mole of the diol (M = 62 g mol⁻¹).
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.2 g halves the amount; 9.2 g is the mass of ethanol (a single –OH), not the diol; 24.8 g doubles the amount.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', chemical properties of alkenes (oxidation with Baeyer's reagent)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Addition of HI to propene gives 2-iodopropane as the main product even in the presence of a peroxide.
Reason (R): Iodine free radicals formed under these conditions combine with one another to give iodine molecules instead of adding to the double bond.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why the peroxide effect is shown by HBr but not by HI
solution.explanation: The anti-Markovnikov (peroxide) effect needs halogen free radicals to add to the alkene. With HI the H–I bond (296.8 kJ mol⁻¹) is weak, but the iodine atoms formed combine to give I₂ rather than adding to C=C, so the ionic Markovnikov addition continues and gives 2-iodopropane. R is the reason for A.
steps: Peroxide → radicals; with HI, I• + I• → I₂
No radical chain addition → Markovnikov product
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes (peroxide effect)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following alkyl halides undergoes dehydrohalogenation fastest when heated with alcoholic KOH?

solution.concept: Rate of dehydrohalogenation
solution.explanation: NCERT states that the rate of dehydrohalogenation depends on both the halogen (iodine > bromine > chlorine) and the alkyl group (tertiary > secondary > primary). A tertiary iodide combines the best of both.
solution.why_others_wrong: (CH₃)₃CCl has the less reactive halogen; 1-iodobutane and 1-chlorobutane are primary.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', preparation of alkenes (dehydrohalogenation)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the reaction in List-I with the type of reaction in List-II.

List-I:
A. n-Hexane heated at 773 K and 10–20 atm over Cr₂O₃ on alumina → benzene
B. CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O (a few drops of conc. H₂SO₄) → CH₃CH₂OH
C. (CH₃)₃C–Br + alcoholic KOH → (CH₃)₂C=CH₂
D. Ethyne passed through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K → benzene

List-II:
I. β-Elimination
II. Cyclic polymerisation
III. Aromatisation
IV. Addition

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Types of reactions of hydrocarbons
solution.explanation: Alkanes with six or more carbon atoms are converted into benzene and its homologues over Cr₂O₃/V₂O₅/Mo₂O₃ (aromatisation). Alkenes add water in the presence of acid (Markovnikov addition). Alkyl halides lose HX from adjacent carbons with alcoholic KOH (β-elimination). Three ethyne molecules combine at 873 K over red-hot iron to form benzene (cyclic polymerisation).
solution.why_others_wrong: Both A and D give benzene, but A starts from an alkane (aromatisation) and D joins three ethyne molecules (polymerisation); the other codes also confuse addition with elimination.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', chemical properties of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Ethyne is hydrated by passing it into dilute sulphuric acid containing mercuric sulphate at 333 K. The mass of the carbonyl compound formed from 5.2 g of ethyne, assuming complete conversion, is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.concept: Hydration of alkynes
solution.explanation: Water adds across the triple bond to give an unstable enol, CH₂=CHOH, which changes into ethanal, CH₃CHO (M = 44 g mol⁻¹). One mole of ethyne gives one mole of ethanal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.2 g is for ethanol and 12.0 g for ethanoic acid, neither of which is formed; 4.4 g halves the amount.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', chemical properties of alkynes (addition of water)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the presence of ultraviolet light, benzene adds chlorine to give benzene hexachloride, C₆H₆Cl₆. The mass of benzene hexachloride formed from 7.8 g of benzene, assuming complete reaction, is (C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5):

solution.concept: Addition reactions of benzene
solution.explanation: Under UV light and heat benzene undergoes addition rather than substitution: C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆ (M = 72 + 6 + 213 = 291 g mol⁻¹).
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.25 g is the mass of chlorobenzene, the substitution product formed in the dark with a Lewis acid; 22.00 g adds only two Cl₂; 14.55 g halves the answer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', chemical properties of benzene (addition reactions)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Naphthalene, C₁₀H₈, is a planar molecule made of two fused benzene rings, with every ring carbon atom sp² hybridised and π electrons delocalised over both rings. The number of π electrons in naphthalene and the value of n for which it satisfies Hückel's (4n + 2) rule are, respectively:

solution.concept: Hückel's rule
solution.explanation: A Kekulé-type structure of naphthalene has five C=C bonds, i.e. 10 π electrons. Setting 4n + 2 = 10 gives n = 2, so naphthalene satisfies the (4n + 2) π-electron condition for aromaticity.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 π electrons would need six double bonds; 8 is the count for a 4n system; n = 3 corresponds to 14 π electrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', aromaticity (Hückel rule)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Cyclohexene is treated with ozone and the ozonide formed is decomposed with zinc dust and water. The product is:

solution.concept: Ozonolysis of a cyclic alkene
solution.explanation: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond and turns each doubly bonded carbon into a C=O group. In a ring, both new carbonyl groups stay in the same molecule, so the ring opens into a single six-carbon chain with an aldehyde group at each end. Zn/H₂O prevents further oxidation to acids.
steps: Ring opens: one product, not two
solution.why_others_wrong: Cyclohexanone would keep the ring; two propanal molecules would need two separate fragments; hexanedioic acid requires oxidative work-up, not zinc and water.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', ozonolysis of alkenes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Calcium carbide reacts with water to give X. X is hydrogenated with H₂ over palladium on charcoal partly deactivated with quinoline, giving Y. Y adds HBr to give Z, and Z is heated with sodium in dry ether to give W. W is:

solution.concept: Sequence of reactions of ethyne
solution.explanation: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → HC≡CH (X). Lindlar's catalyst stops hydrogenation at the alkene: CH₂=CH₂ (Y). HBr adds to give CH₃CH₂Br (Z). The Wurtz reaction joins two ethyl groups: CH₃CH₂–CH₂CH₃, butane (W).
solution.why_others_wrong: Ethane would need complete hydrogenation and no coupling; but-2-ene is not formed in a Wurtz reaction; hexane would need a three-carbon halide.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', preparation and properties of alkynes, alkenes and alkanes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Hydrogenation of ethyne over Lindlar's catalyst (palladised charcoal deactivated with quinoline) gives ethane.
Statement II: Cyclohexene decolourises a solution of bromine in CCl₄, but benzene does not under the same conditions.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Partial hydrogenation of alkynes; addition reactions of alkenes versus benzene
solution.explanation: The partly poisoned palladium catalyst stops hydrogenation of an alkyne at the alkene stage, so ethyne gives ethene, not ethane (Statement I false). Cyclohexene has a localised C=C bond and adds bromine readily, whereas benzene, stabilised by delocalisation of its π electrons, does not add bromine in CCl₄ (Statement II true).
steps: Lindlar's catalyst → alkene only → Statement I false
Alkene adds Br₂; aromatic benzene resists addition → Statement II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', preparation of alkenes from alkynes; properties of benzene
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
n-Hexane is heated at 773 K under 10–20 atm over Cr₂O₃ supported on alumina and is converted into benzene:
C₆H₁₄ → C₆H₆ + 4H₂
If 8.6 g of n-hexane is used and the yield of benzene is 80%, the volume of hydrogen released, measured at STP, is (C = 12, H = 1; molar volume at STP = 22.4 L mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Aromatisation of alkanes
solution.explanation: Each mole of n-hexane converted into benzene releases four moles of hydrogen. Only 80% of the hexane is converted.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.96 L ignores the 80% yield; 5.38 L releases three H₂ per hexane; 1.79 L releases one.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Hydrocarbons', chemical properties of alkanes (aromatisation)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In how many of the following compounds is the halogen atom bonded to an sp²-hybridised carbon atom?
CH₂=CHCl, C₆H₅Cl, C₆H₅CH₂Cl, CH₂=CH–CH₂Cl, CH₃–CH=CH–Br, (CH₃)₃C–Cl, 4-chlorotoluene (Cl on the ring)

solution.concept: Classification of halogen compounds by the hybridisation of the C–X carbon
solution.explanation: Vinylic halides (X on a C=C carbon) and aryl halides (X on a ring carbon) have the halogen on an sp² carbon. In allylic and benzylic halides the halogen is on an sp³ carbon next to the C=C or the ring.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 wrongly counts the benzylic or allylic chloride (the CH₂ bearing Cl is sp³); 2 or 3 miss 4-chlorotoluene or 1-bromoprop-1-ene.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', classification (compounds containing sp³ and sp² C–X bonds)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The first chlorinated organic insecticide, originally prepared in 1873, whose effectiveness as an insecticide was discovered only in 1939, is:

solution.concept: Polyhalogen compounds: DDT
solution.explanation: NCERT describes DDT (p,p′-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) as the first chlorinated organic insecticide. It was prepared in 1873, but its insecticidal action was discovered by Paul Müller in 1939.
solution.why_others_wrong: Freon-12 is a refrigerant, chloroform a solvent and former anaesthetic, iodoform an antiseptic.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Haloalkanes and Haloarenes', polyhalogen compounds (DDT)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Grignard reagents are obtained by treating haloalkanes with magnesium metal in dry ether.
